philanthropic

/fil-uhn-THROP-ik/ - the stress falls on THROP · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Philanthropic means devoted to helping others through charitable gifts of money or resources.

The bakery keeps a quiet philanthropic ledger — every unsold loaf is driven to the shelter before the ovens have cooled.

Example

The retired ferry captain turned philanthropic in her seventies, funding swimming lessons for every child in the harbor district — 'the sea took my friends,' she said; 'it won't take theirs.'

Philanthropic is more precise than 'kind' or 'generous' because it describes organized giving aimed at strangers' welfare — scholarships, shelters, vaccination drives — usually with money and at scale. Kindness happens across a table; philanthropy writes a check that outlives the writer.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

altruistic: Altruistic means putting other people's good ahead of your own, in any currency — time, sleep, safety, money. Philanthropic is narrower and better funded: organized giving, usually of money and at scale. A broke volunteer can be perfectly altruistic; philanthropic implies resources behind the generosity.

public-spirited: Public-spirited means working for the community as a whole — parks, petitions, school boards — usually by donating time and effort. Philanthropic aims wide too, but it flows through wealth: donations, endowments, funded programs. The public-spirited citizen shows up; the philanthropic one writes the check that builds the hall.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

miserly: hoards what it could give

self-serving: arranges everything, even gifts, to profit itself

Where it sits · how organized and far-reaching the giving is — kindly → openhanded → philanthropic

kindly vs. philanthropic: A kindly person is warm to those in reach — a smaller circle than philanthropic, which organizes help for strangers it will never meet.

openhanded vs. philanthropic: Openhanded giving is personal and free with what it has — picking up checks, lending easily — but it stops short of philanthropic, which builds the giving into institutions: funds, scholarships, wings of hospitals.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — phil-

Root — phil-: to love (Greek philein)

Root — anthrop-

Root — anthrop-: human being (Greek anthropos)

Suffix — -ic

Suffix — -ic: characteristic of

Put it together

Put it together: Phil- (Greek philein, 'to love') + anthrop- (Greek anthropos, 'human being') + -ic = characteristic of loving humankind. The Greeks meant the temperament; English aimed it at the wallet. A philanthropic foundation is, letter for letter, a machine built to love people in general — which is why the word suits donors better than friends.

Use the root in a new word: anthropology

Use the root in a new word: anthropology: Her anthropology fieldwork compared how three fishing cultures divide a day's catch.

Word Choice

formal / institutional

Philanthropic suits organized generosity — foundations, endowments, galas. For one warm act, 'kind' or 'generous' rings truer; calling a borrowed pencil philanthropic is a joke. Keep the contrast with its unit-mate mutualistic sharp: mutualistic exchanges flow both ways by definition, while philanthropic giving expects the ledger never to balance.
